headline: Active ETFs have grown in AUM but lost market share, remaining below 20% of the ETF market as passive continues to dominate
reasoning: While active ETFs have attracted new players and seen funds under management growth, their share of the overall ETF market has not kept pace with passive growth and has stayed below the 20% mark. Monfort suggests this ~20% level may represent a natural equilibrium between active and passive in the ETF wrapper. Passive players also tend to dominate thematic launches, moving quickly when a new trend emerges.
quote: You could say that the actives have been having a great play at it because they have seen funds under management growth. There's been a lot of new players coming to the market as well, but in terms of their share, they've just not been growing as fast as the passive players out there. And the passive players tend to dominate a lot of like thematics. As soon as something happens, they'll come out with a play. But as we you can see here, the orange line is showing the actual growth. But in terms of share of market in the blue, it has sort of remained underneath that 20% mark, which is maybe the right place that they need to be at for an equilibrium.
episode_title: $360B and counting: Australia’s ETF market turns 25

headline: ETF investor behaviour is trend-chasing: ESG dominated for years, then gold and precious metals, now AI and SpaceX are the hottest themes
reasoning: Monfort observes that ETF inflows tend to chase the dominant theme of the moment — ESG was the major theme for several years, followed by a gold and precious metals rush, and most recently AI and SpaceX-related products. ETF issuers respond to these trends by launching new thematic products after prices have already run up. This pattern reveals what investors were most excited about at each point in time and suggests a follow-the-trend dynamic rather than forward-looking positioning.
quote: It tells us that ETFs tend to follow the dominant theme at the time, whether it was ESG for a number of years. And we've seen that in previous years when we've analyzed what the major themes were. But it also tells us that when things happened, like the gold rush that we saw in recent times that people followed that precious metals, as we can see there. More recently, AI and SpaceX have been the major players. But in terms of the lookback that we've had, now that we can look at 25 years of data, we do see that people tend to follow a theme. The ETF issuers provide these new themes after something has hit, whether it's the highs and the crypto price, whether it is something new happening and a whole lot of companies going into ESG for a number of years, that was the play.
episode_title: $360B and counting: Australia’s ETF market turns 25

headline: Strong product lineup and willingness to close underperforming themes have allowed rapid market share gains; Nasdaq and ASX 200 products among the most commonly held in retail portfolios
reasoning: Monfort attributes BetaShares' outsized market share growth to a combination of strong marketing and a well-designed product suite. A key differentiator is BetaShares' discipline in closing thematic ETFs when trends fade, rather than allowing zombie funds to persist. Their Nasdaq and ASX 200 ETFs are among the most commonly held products in retail investor portfolios tracked by ETF tracker analytics. The A200 product overtook State Street's STW in AUM, which Monfort links partly to fee competition.
quote: Beta shares have just been able to grow at a really fast pace. The investments that they've made, whether it is on the marketing side, whether it is the ETFs that they've got there, they also are one of those that as soon as the theme is not working, they end up closing it quite well. You can see here on screen that beta shares at 200 is really interesting. Despite not being the largest ASX 200 play that you had a few years ago. It's 12 XT in terms of its size. Um, Nasdaq is also another beta shares play. And when I look at ETF tracker, for example, the most common holdings that people have when they create their portfolios, it is those big plays like Nasdaq or S&P 500 or the 800. Those are the ones that people most commonly hold, at least in my analytics portfolio.
episode_title: $360B and counting: Australia’s ETF market turns 25

headline: Australia's ETF market has quadrupled to $360B in six years, driven by concentration in major passive index products from advisors and superannuation funds
reasoning: Mark Monfort notes that the Australian ETF market, which launched in 2001, has seen its assets under management nearly quadruple to $360 billion, with growth concentrated in major index ETFs such as ASX 200 and broad market plays. Financial advisors and superannuation funds are the key buyers, typically using a hub-and-satellite approach. The number of funds has roughly doubled from 215 in 2020, while AUM has grown much faster, reflecting concentration in the largest funds.
quote: The growth has been from the majors. It's been the Vas, the 200. The major index plays that typically people have in their sort of like hub and satellite type approach to ETFs, whether it's from financial advisors, the superannuation funds also buying into ETFs, they all appear to be concentrated. As we can see the growth here on the screen, they all appear to be concentrated in those major names.
episode_title: $360B and counting: Australia’s ETF market turns 25
